newsitem.title: USA: Gambling executives shrug off threat from Hilton/ITT.
newsitem.headline: Gambling executives shrug off threat from Hilton/ITT.

text.p: Casino industry executives said Friday they were sticking close to their own strategies as they face the competitive specter of a merged Hilton Hotel Corp. and ITT Corp.
As the saying goes at poker tables in Las Vegas, a good player has to know when to fold a hand and when to hold on, and many of the executives apparently have decided to hold.

Hilton's proposed $6.5 billion acquisition of ITT would create a hotel and casino giant with 30 casinos and roughly $2.5 billion in annual cash flow, making it three to five times the size of its nearest rival.
But competitors in the hotly contested major gambling markets aren't shaking in their boots. Instead, they said they will play hard and fast if the merger is completed.

"We don't subscribe to the idea that size for size sake is the end game here," said Glenn Schaeffer, president of Circus Circus Enterprises Inc. "We think it is possessing the resources to do big things in major markets, and we control those markets and we control those resources."

Indeed, the winning hands in recent years in Las Vegas and Atlantic City, N.J., have been held by companies with huge, themed casinos that cost hundreds of millions of dollars and attracted visitors worldwide.
Major operators like Circus Circus, Mirage Resorts Inc., MGM Grand Inc. and Harrah's Entertainment Inc., possess the muscle to build such huge attractions.

Hilton officials maintain the merger with ITT would lower its cost of capital, giving the company greater borrowing power and boosting profit margins. But several top executives at rival operators dismissed such claims, saying their cost of capital was roughly the same as Hilton's.
"The only time cost of capital makes a big difference is on long-term debt. It doesn't really matter," said a high-ranking executive of one rival company.
Long-term debt ratings for Hilton and ITT are roughly equal to those of the other major companies.
Moody's Investors Service Inc., for instance, rates senior debt of Hilton and ITT at "Baa1." Circus and Mirage are at "Baa2". All are investment grade.
A Hilton and ITT combination would save the companies some $100 million in costs, but those are internal to the company and do not affect the way other operators work, experts said.
"Being larger doesn't mean they'll be a more effective competitor," said Shannon Bybee, a gambling industry expert at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.
Indeed, simply setting up slot machines and blackjack tables and operating at higher profit margins does not guarantee success in Las Vegas.

For example, Stratosphere Corp., which had hoped to attract gamblers to its Las Vegas casino by erecting the largest tower west of the Mississippi, recently was forced to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection this week after substantial losses.

While some market players have speculated that mid-tier gambling companies such as Stations Casinos Inc. or Rio Hotels Inc. might feel competitive heat from a giant like Hilton and ITT, experts disagree.
Those mid-level companies generally compete for local customer traffic instead of the high-rolling and overseas gamblers who frequent Hilton's and Caesars' operations.

Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach has said he wants Hilton to be the biggest company in what he calls a consolidating industry. But several executives dispute the notion of consolidation in the gambling industry.

Like others, Circus Circus' Schaeffer argued that the factors driving consolidation involve cost savings, capital access and obtaining management talent, all of which executives from the majors believe they currently possess.

Ironically, several industry executives and experts would welcome the ITT/Hilton combination. They note that Hilton has said it will review ITT's current construction plans in Las Vegas and Atlantic City, a move that would likely lead to fewer properties and less competition.
Also, they like the attention that Hilton's hostile takeover has focused on the gambling industry, which has in the past week has helped drive up the price of many companies' stocks.
